background.definition: Acute mastoiditis is an inflammatory, often destructive, condition of the mastoid bone and air cell system characterized by otalgia, postauricular pain, and fever.

list.listitem: Acute mastoiditis occurs in 1.2 to 9.2 cases per 100,000 persons per year.
Although the incidence has decreased with the use of antibiotics for the treatment of otitis media, acute mastoiditis still complicates between 1 in 250 to 1 in 2287 cases of acute otitis media.
Recent studies indicate that the rate of mastoiditis may be increasing slightly with decreasing use of antibiotics for the treatment of acute otitis media.

A retrospective cohort study of patients seen by British GPs from 1982 to 2012 found that antibiotic treatment of AOM reduced odds of developing acute mastoiditis with a NNT of 2181 (95% CI, 1196-5709).
Please see for bacteriologic causes of mastoiditis.
The epitympanic recess of the middle ear connects to the mastoid air cells by means of the aditus ad antrum.
During a case of acute otitis media, exudate from the middle ear follows this connection into the mastoid air cells.
Acute mastoiditis occurs when this exudate causes mastoid inflammation or destruction of the bony trabeculae.
Acute mastoiditis usually occurs after 10 to 14 days of middle ear symptoms, but may also be a primary infection in the absence of abnormal middle ear findings.

A systematic review identified 24 RCTs and observational studies comparing antibiotics with placebo for children with acute otitis media. They found a lower risk of mastoiditis as a complication (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.59, NNT = 5368). Overall incidence was only 0.02%. This tiny benefit must be weighed against harms of antibiotics including C. difficile infection. B

Acute mastoiditis is a clinical diagnosis suggested by symptoms such as otalgia, postauricular pain, and fever. Frequent signs include an abnormal tympanic membrane and postauricular swelling, tenderness, and erythema. C

Order a CT scan for patients with suspected intracranial complications, those requiring mastoidectomy, and those who do not respond to conservative therapy. In addition, a CT scan should be considered in all patients with suspected mastoiditis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Normal tympanic membrane, associated skin lesion
Langerhans cells on biopsy, typical plain film findings
Absence of general lymphadenopathy or abnormal cell lines on CBC
Normal tympanic membrane, associated scalp or skin lesion
No postauricular swelling, erythema, or tenderness

list.listitem: Otalgia, fever, and a recent diagnosis of otitis media are the most common historical clues.

Physical examination often reveals an abnormal tympanic membrane, postauricular swelling, erythema, tenderness, and a protruding pinna. Please see for the frequency of signs and symptoms in patients with mastoiditis.
Antibiotic treatment for otitis media may mask the classic presentation of acute mastoiditis, requiring a higher degree of awareness on the part of clinicians.
Common, nonspecific laboratory findings include leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Order CT for patients with suspected intracranial complications to assess whether coalescence of mastroid trabeculae has occurred in those requiring mastoidectomy and in those who do not respond to conservative therapy. In addition, a CT scan should be considered in all patients with suspected mastoiditis.
Middle ear or mastoid cell cultures may help target antibiotic therapy, but can be negative 30% to 40% of the time.
MRI may be useful for evaluating complications such as abscess formation, but is not the preferred modality for assessment of the mastoid.
See algorithm in .
IV antibiotic therapy, with tympanocentesis or myringotomy with or without tube placement, is the initial treatment of choice for uncomplicated acute mastoiditis. B
Appropriate antibiotics include IV cefuroxime, ampicillin with clavulanate, and ceftriaxone for 7 to 10 days followed by oral antibiotics for a total of 4 weeks. B
IV antibiotic therapy, with tympanocentesis or myringotomy with or without tube placement, is the initial treatment of choice for uncomplicated acute mastoiditis.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (n=990) of medical therapy alone found an average cure rate of 72%.
Antibiotic choice should cover gram positive cocci, including penicillin-resistant strains. Examples of appropriate choices include cefuroxime, ampicillin with clavulanate, and ceftriaxone.
IV antibiotics should be started at the time of diagnosis and continued for 7 to 10 days. Afterward, the improving patient may be given oral antibiotics to complete a 4-week treatment course.
Although pseudomonas is isolated from some middle ear and mastoid cavities, the majority of patients respond without antipseudomonal antibiotic therapy.

A study of a UK database with 2.6 million children in general practice found that only one-third had a diagnosis of otitis media in the previous 3 months, and that one would have to treat nearly 5000 children with antibiotics to prevent one episode of mastroiditis (best case).A systematic review of clinical trials comparing antibiotics with placebo or observation in kids with otitis media found only one case of mastoiditis, and that was in a child who received antibiotics.
Tympanocentesis or myringotomy with or without tube placement, in addition to IV antibiotics, are part of the initial treatment of uncomplicated acute mastoiditis.

Mastoidectomy is indicated in patients with a poor response to conservative therapy, who do not improve within 36 to 48 hours of targeted antibiotic therapy, or who present with a subperiosteal abscess, cholesteatoma, facial nerve paralysis, or other complication.

In addition to complications, the need for surgery is predicted by postauricular mass on physical examination and bony destruction on CT scan. It is also more likely in children with longer duration of symptoms (>6 days), elevated WBC, and elevated CRP.
Patients with truly uncomplicated acute mastoiditis (without evidence of bony erosion, intracranial complication, or subperiosteal abscess) may not require mastoidectomy.

Patients with mastoiditis should be hospitalized for IV antibiotic therapy to monitor response to treatment and to evaluate for complications such as subperiosteal abscess, sinus thrombosis, meningitis, labyrinthitis, petrositis, and facial nerve palsy.
Mastoiditis is thought to respond better when treated early, and hearing defects may be reversible. C

algorithm.title: Treatment Approach for the Patient With Acute Mastoiditis.

cell.label: Acute mastoiditis suspected (otalgia, fever, postauricular swelling, tenderness, and/or erythema present).
Hospitalize. Begin IV antibiotic therapy. Monitor for complications.
Is there evidence of complication (subperiosteal abscess, sinus thrombosis, meningitis, labyrinthitis, petrositis, facial nerve palsy)?
Strongly consider imaging screen for occult complications.
Continue IV antibiotics. Monitor for complications.
Refer for myringotomy. Continue IV antibiotics. Monitor for complications.
Obtain appropriate imaging temporal HR-CT to screen for bony opacification, bony destruction, coalescence. Cranial CT with contrast for intracranial complications.
